newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch call money still low ahead of quota expiry.
newsitem.headline: Dutch call money still low ahead of quota expiry.

text.p: Dutch call money rates were still trading below usual levels on Tuesday and dealers said overnight money would probably linger at the current low until Friday's expiry of the three-month secured loans quota.

Most market players were overwhelmed with liquidity as they had been saving more liquidity than needed under the current quota. The quota or limit sets a daily average for commercial banks' borrowing at the central bank at the secured loans rate.
The secured loans has been pegged at 2.50 percent since March 11, while call money was bid as low as 2.25 percent.
Earlier this month call money was bid at with an occasional peak at 3.12 percent bid.
Dealers said call money rates would climb higher when the new credit quota starts running.
Business was thin in the money market, with investors showing little interest in deposits and Dutch Treasury (DTCs).
The price of the June DTCs was set at 3.10 percent and the December contracts were priced at 3.23 percent.
One dealer said that current prices were not interesting for investors.
Dealers said there was no business at all in the Interbank OverNight Average (AIONA) Swap, since the yield curve in the money market was too flat.
"A flat curve is not a good seed-bed for AIONA Swaps," said one.
The current low of call is only temporary and this means that the gap between six-month deposits and call money is usually only some 20 basis points.
The AIONA was introduced last February, just after the Dutch central bank said out would publish an overnight AIBOR (Overnight Amsterdam Interbank Offered Rate).
The AIBOR, currently set at 2.62 percent, is needed for business related to index-swaps and other derivatives.
The guilder was fractionally stronger versus the German mark today, trading at 112.4125 per 100 marks from 112.43 on Monday.
